paragraphs: Higher-order structures describe relationships that involve more than ordinary pairs of vertices. Their mathematical descriptions often separate information into different levels, leaving practitioners to decide how to combine those levels when working with individual vertices. This paper introduces Collapsed Effective Operators to make that combination part of the operator itself.

The method starts from a graded Laplacian, which represents the structure across its levels, and applies Schur complementation to eliminate higher-order degrees of freedom. The resulting vertex-level operator retains interactions mediated by the higher-order topology. It is generally dense, reflecting connections that can extend beyond immediate neighbors, and the construction applies to arbitrary higher-order structures.

The authors prove that the operator preserves positive semidefiniteness and satisfies a strict spectral upper bound relative to the rank-0 Hodge Laplacian, corresponding to lower system energy under higher-order connectivity. Empirically, it improves spectral clustering and signal smoothing. It also supplies positional encodings for neural networks, giving those networks a direct way to incorporate topological information.
icml-2026-collapsed-effective-operators-.tldr: Collapsed Effective Operators compress higher-order topology into a vertex-level operator that supports clustering, smoothing, and neural positional encodings.

paragraphs: Autonomous systems need to turn observations into actions quickly and with little energy. High-precision neural controllers can make those deployment requirements difficult to meet. This paper introduces Differentiable Weightless Controllers, an architecture designed to learn flexible, nonlinear control policies while producing a particularly efficient hardware implementation.

The central idea is to connect gradient-based learning with symbolic circuit execution. Controllers can be trained end to end using gradient-based techniques, then compiled directly into circuits compatible with field-programmable gate arrays, or FPGAs. The abstract reports action evaluation in a few clock cycles, sometimes just one, with energy costs at the nanojoule level.

Across five MuJoCo benchmarks, including the high-dimensional Humanoid task, these controllers achieve returns competitive with standard full-precision and quantized neural policies. Their connectivity is also structurally sparse and interpretable, allowing inspection of which inputs influence decisions. The findings show that the proposed architecture can combine competitive benchmark control performance with low-cost circuit execution and a more inspectable decision structure.
icml-2026-differentiable-weightless-cont.tldr: Differentiable Weightless Controllers learn competitive continuous-control policies that compile directly into fast, energy-efficient logic circuits.

paragraphs: Neural scaling laws describe regular patterns in how generalization error changes as learning systems scale. This paper studies the dynamics behind those patterns in random-feature regression and the neural network Gaussian process setting. Its goal is to explain how learning evolves over time when the data's kernel eigenvalues follow a power-law distribution.

The authors derive a dynamical mean-field theory that brings several learning regimes into one framework: Bayesian Gaussian process inference, gradient flow with or without weight decay, and stochastic Langevin training. Using statistical-physics methods, they summarize high-dimensional dynamics through a smaller collection of quantities that describe collective behavior.

Within this description, training separates into individual eigenmode dynamics linked through shared response functions and effective noise statistics. This makes it possible to connect the data's spectrum with the changing generalization error. The framework quantitatively explains scaling behavior and early-stopping effects in the studied setting, showing how spectral structure and training dynamics jointly determine learning progress.
icml-2026-dynamics-of-neural-scaling-law.tldr: A unified dynamical theory links power-law data spectra to generalization, neural scaling laws, and early-stopping effects in Gaussian process regression.

paragraphs: Language models can spend many reasoning tokens on even basic arithmetic. The paper identifies number tokenization as a contributor: splitting a single number across several tokens makes numerical processing less compact. That inefficiency matters when models must handle large quantities of numerical data or calculations that consume substantial context.

The authors first specify desirable properties for single-token number encodings and argue that existing approaches do not meet them. They then introduce BitTokens, which represents a number in one token using its IEEE 754 binary floating-point representation. The approach changes how numerical values enter the model, providing a compact representation intended to support effective arithmetic learning.

Experiments show that even small language models using BitTokens can learn algorithms that perform basic arithmetic nearly perfectly. This supports the claim that numerical representation is an important part of efficient calculation. The authors suggest that the resulting efficiency could enable longer and more complex problems; the stated experimental result concerns basic arithmetic, while that broader expansion remains a possibility.
icml-2026-efficient-numeracy-in-language.tldr: BitTokens encodes numbers as single tokens using floating-point bits, enabling small language models to learn nearly perfect basic arithmetic.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce memorized training images, raising privacy and intellectual-property concerns. Some mitigation methods remove weights thought to trigger a particular reproduction. This paper examines the assumption behind that strategy: that memorization can be isolated in a localized set of model weights.

The authors show that small changes to the text embeddings of previously mitigated prompts can bring image replication back after pruning. They also find replication triggers distributed across embedding space, different internal activations for embeddings that reproduce the same image, and disagreement between pruning methods about which weights are responsible. Together, these observations provide multiple indications that memorization is not inherently local.

The paper then demonstrates more robust mitigation through adversarial fine-tuning that bypasses the locality assumption. Its significance is that suppressing a known trigger may leave other routes to the same memorized image intact. The findings support evaluating mitigation beyond its original prompts and developing methods that address the broader behavior revealed by embedding perturbations.
icml-2026-finding-dori-discovery-of-reta.tldr: Small text-embedding changes can restore image replication after pruning, challenging localized accounts of diffusion-model memorization.

paragraphs: Reusing training examples can improve learning efficiency, but the benefit is harder to characterize in nonlinear, nonconvex problems. This paper studies a quadratic single-index model in d dimensions. It compares full-batch gradient descent, which repeatedly uses the dataset, with online stochastic gradient descent, which sees each example only once.

For the original quadratic activation, one-pass SGD needs on the order of d log d samples for weak recovery. The authors show that full-batch spherical gradient descent on correlation loss retains this logarithmic factor. With a truncated activation, however, full-batch gradient descent has a favorable optimization landscape at roughly d samples and outperforms one-pass SGD using that same activation.

A complementary trajectory analysis studies full-batch gradient descent on squared loss from a small initialization. In that setting, roughly d samples and log d gradient steps suffice for exact recovery. These results identify concrete conditions under which repeated data use provides a statistical advantage, while showing that the activation, loss, and initialization matter to the guarantees.
icml-2026-full-batch-gradient-descent-ou.tldr: For a studied single-index problem, full-batch gradient descent can achieve recovery with fewer samples than one-pass SGD under specified training choices.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders can expose labeled concepts inside language models, but visual concepts are harder to label unambiguously. VISTA transfers an existing language-based interpretation system into vision. In a LLaVA-style vision-language model, it constrains the visual projector to place image tokens into the language model's already labeled sparse-autoencoder space.

The projector is regularized with the language autoencoder's reconstruction loss, avoiding the need to train a separate visual autoencoder. The authors report a threefold increase in the matching rate between strongly activated textual concepts and semantic elements present in an image. They also compare spatial localization across vision encoders, finding stronger localization from DINOv2 features.

The authors test the alignment through localized interventions that remove or replace objects in the model's perception while preserving surrounding content. They report improvements of 35% for removal and 47% for replacement over vision-only baselines. Validated across multiple language-model architectures, these interventions provide causal evidence that visual representations occupy the textual concept space, beyond merely producing plausible descriptive labels.
icml-2026-interpretability-transfer-from.tldr: VISTA aligns visual tokens with an existing textual sparse-autoencoder space, improving concept interpretation and localized interventions.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can connect an image encoder to a language model through a shallow mapping, yet understanding what the resulting visual tokens mean throughout processing remains difficult. LatentLens addresses this by translating internal visual representations into natural-language descriptions at different layers of the language model.

The method first encodes a large text corpus and stores the internal representation of each token in its textual context. It then compares visual token representations with this collection and uses the nearest contextualized text representations as descriptions. Because the reference tokens carry context, the resulting interpretations can express finer semantic distinctions than isolated vocabulary tokens.

Across 15 vision-language models, the authors find that most visual tokens are interpretable at every studied layer using LatentLens. Common methods such as LogitLens substantially underestimate that interpretability in the comparison. Qualitative examples show semantically meaningful, detailed descriptions. The findings provide evidence of alignment between vision and language representations and make that alignment easier to inspect throughout the model's processing.
icml-2026-latentlens-revealing-highly-in.tldr: LatentLens describes visual tokens using nearby contextualized text representations, revealing interpretability across all studied layers of 15 vision-language models.

paragraphs: Combining multiple experts with parameter-efficient fine-tuning often requires a separate adapter for each expert. That makes the trainable parameter count grow with the number of experts. LiME replaces these replicated adapters with one shared fine-tuning module whose output is adjusted by small expert-specific vectors.

Expert specialization therefore comes from lightweight modulation. Routing uses existing frozen and adapted representations, adding no learned router parameters. LiME also incorporates routing over n-gram windows and a mechanism that chooses how many experts to use according to routing confidence. The authors prove information-preservation benefits from more experts and a bounded-error approximation to full expert-specific fine-tuning within their theoretical treatment.

On MMT-47, a benchmark covering 47 text, image, and video tasks, LiME achieves competitive or better performance than corresponding mixture-of-experts fine-tuning baselines. It uses up to four times fewer trainable parameters and trains up to 29% faster. These results support shared-module modulation as an efficient way to obtain task specialization without duplicating an entire adaptation module for every expert.
icml-2026-lime-lightweight-mixture-of-ex.tldr: LiME creates lightweight experts around one shared fine-tuning module, reducing trainable parameters and training time while maintaining competitive multimodal performance.

paragraphs: In truncated regression, a sample is visible only when its outcome falls inside a survival set. Estimating the underlying regression relationship is especially difficult when that set is unknown, because the learner must account for a selection rule it cannot directly inspect. Earlier algorithms for this case required restrictive feature distributions and unfavorable runtime dependence on accuracy.

The paper gives an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in d divided by the target error, where d is the number of regression coefficients. It allows sub-Gaussian feature vectors, expanding beyond the Gaussian feature assumption used in earlier approaches. This combines a broader feature-distribution setting with a substantially improved computational guarantee.

A central ingredient is a procedure for learning unions of a bounded number of intervals from positive examples alone. Its guarantee requires a smoothness condition, which is a stated part of the result. Besides supporting unknown-truncation regression, that procedure contributes to positive-only PAC learning, where the learner must infer a set without examples explicitly labeled as outside it.
icml-2026-linear-regression-with-unknown.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm for unknown-truncation linear regression with sub-Gaussian features, using a positive-only interval-learning subroutine.

paragraphs: Mechanical engineering drawings pose challenges beyond ordinary image questions. Dense annotations, projection rules, geometric constraints, and specialized knowledge all affect how a drawing should be read. The paper introduces MechVQA to evaluate these abilities systematically and to support improvements in multimodal language models for this domain.

The dataset is built through a semi-automated construction and quality-control process. It contains 3.3 thousand densely annotated pictures and 21 thousand question–answer pairs. Its ten tasks span recognition, reasoning, and judging, allowing evaluation to cover both identifying drawing content and making more demanding inferences about it.

The authors also develop MechVL through multiple training stages as a specialized baseline. In their experiments, it exceeds the strongest closed-source baseline by 7.57 percentage points on the benchmark's total score. The dataset and model together provide a reusable foundation for studying mechanical drawing understanding. The reported gain demonstrates stronger performance on this evaluation and supports further development toward mechanical design and inspection applications.
icml-2026-mechvqa-benchmarking-and-enhan.tldr: MechVQA benchmarks mechanical drawing understanding, and the specialized MechVL model improves its total score over the strongest closed-source baseline.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations by training with objectives that incorporate physical constraints. Although they can be powerful scientific tools, their behavior is difficult to interpret. This paper introduces PINNfluence to connect their predictions and training losses back to the data points used during learning.

The framework adapts influence functions to the composite objectives used by physics-informed networks. These objectives contain multiple components, so attribution must account for more than a single undifferentiated training loss. PINNfluence provides fine-grained relationships among individual data points, loss components, and predictions, offering a structured way to examine how training information affects the learned solution.

Experiments across several partial differential equations show that influence patterns distinguish structural characteristics of well-trained and poorly trained networks. This turns attribution into a diagnostic tool for examining successful and unsuccessful training behavior. The contribution is an explicit interpretation framework grounded in training data, providing a route toward understanding and improving reliability beyond analyzing failures only after they appear.
icml-2026-pinnfluence-interpreting-pinns.tldr: PINNfluence adapts influence functions to physics-informed networks, linking predictions and loss components to training points for detailed diagnostics.

paragraphs: Relational foundation models learn from databases containing multiple connected tables, but privacy restrictions make diverse training databases difficult to obtain. Generating more rows in an isolated table does not address the structure connecting tables. PluRel tackles this problem by synthesizing complete relational databases from scratch.

The framework builds databases in three stages. Directed graphs describe the schema, bipartite graphs specify primary-key and foreign-key connections between tables, and conditional causal mechanisms generate table features. Separating these stages provides a broad design space for varying both database structure and contents while keeping generation computationally lightweight.

Using these synthetic databases, the authors observe power-law relationships between pretraining loss and both database count and total pretraining tokens. Increasing the number of synthetic databases also improves generalization to real databases, and synthetic pretraining produces strong starting models for continued training on real data. These empirical findings support synthetic database diversity as a promising way to scale relational-model training when public real-world databases are scarce.
icml-2026-plurel-synthetic-data-unlocks-.tldr: PluRel generates diverse connected databases, revealing empirical scaling laws and improved transfer from synthetic pretraining to real relational data.

paragraphs: Small models deployed on premises often receive supervised fine-tuning without subsequent preference alignment. Human preference labels and maintained reward models can be too costly for these settings. This paper proposes a positive–unlabeled distillation method that obtains a training signal from a teacher's generated responses without either of those resources.

For each prompt, the method queries the teacher once to obtain an anchor response. The local student generates several candidates, then uses anchor-conditioned self-ranking to derive pairwise or listwise preferences. Those preferences support local optimization through direct preference optimization or group relative policy optimization, keeping the iterative training loop local after obtaining the teacher anchors.

The theoretical analysis supports the induced signal's order consistency and its concentration on near-optimal candidates, providing a justification for stable preference optimization. Experiments report consistently strong performance in a low-cost setting. The approach matters because it turns limited black-box teacher access into a reusable local preference signal, extending small-model adaptation beyond supervised examples without requiring a separate reward model.
icml-2026-positiveunlabeled-reinforcemen.tldr: One teacher response per prompt anchors local student self-ranking, enabling low-cost preference optimization without human preference labels or a reward model.

paragraphs: Proteins often function by moving between different conformations, so predicting a single structure does not establish whether a model captures biologically relevant dynamics. ProMiSE provides a dataset and evaluation scheme for testing multiple protein states within native biological assemblies, bringing several causes of conformational change into one benchmark.

The benchmark covers intrinsic changes as well as changes induced by ligands or other proteins. The authors evaluate leading structure-prediction systems, including AlphaFold3 and recent generative approaches. They find limited sampling of intrinsic alternative states and frequent insensitivity to biological context in cases where surrounding molecules should help determine the conformation.

Analysis of internal representations suggests that exposure to training data can favor dominant conformations over other relevant states, primarily through the structure module. Results from BioEmu indicate that reducing bias during decoding can substantially improve multi-state sampling without major changes to upstream pair representations. This identifies decoding behavior as a promising intervention point while grounding evaluation in biological context and functionally meaningful alternatives.
icml-2026-promise-protein-multi-state-ev.tldr: ProMiSE benchmarks biologically relevant protein states and finds shortcomings in current models, with decoding bias emerging as a promising improvement target.

paragraphs: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures learn representations that remain consistent across views of an input. Distribution-matching regularization can prevent these representations from collapsing, but common Gaussian targets favor dense features. This paper introduces a target distribution and regularizer designed to make sparsity an explicit, controllable part of representation learning.

Rectified Distribution Matching Regularization aligns representations with a Rectified Generalized Gaussian distribution through a sliced two-sample loss. Rectification controls the expected number of nonzero components. The distribution's continuous truncated component also has a maximum-entropy characterization under specified expected norm and support constraints, giving the design a principled statistical basis.

Adding this regularizer produces Rectified LpJEPA, which strictly generalizes earlier Gaussian-based JEPAs. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show sparse, non-negative representations with favorable trade-offs between sparsity and performance, alongside competitive downstream results. The findings indicate that distribution matching can enforce a desired representation structure while retaining useful task information, making sparsity a feature of the training objective rather than an incidental outcome.
icml-2026-rectified-lpjepa-joint-embeddi.tldr: Rectified LpJEPA uses a controllable sparse target distribution to learn non-negative representations while preserving competitive image-classification performance.

paragraphs: Open-ended tasks are difficult to improve through reinforcement learning because there may be no exact answer checker. Rubric Curriculum RL uses the gap between judging and generating: a model may be better at recognizing a stronger response than producing one initially. The method requires no new data, human annotations, or stronger teacher.

RcRL combines pairwise comparisons of generated responses with a curriculum over rubric criteria. Pairwise preferences supply a more discriminative signal than absolute scores, while changing the objective over training helps reduce reward hacking. In the reported experiments, it preserves output entropy and continues improving beyond 1,000 steps, whereas baselines plateau or collapse within a few hundred.

For creative writing, RcRL outputs are preferred over the base model 70.5% of the time, with gains across multiple benchmarks and judges. On HealthBench, reported improvements are 14.6% on the full set and 25.4% on the consensus subset. These findings support structured, evolving self-evaluation as a way to sustain improvement where exact verification is unavailable.
icml-2026-rubric-curriculum-rl-exploitin.tldr: RcRL combines pairwise self-evaluation with changing rubric criteria to sustain improvement on open-ended tasks without new annotations or stronger teachers.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a small part of a pretrained model can be sufficient for adaptation, even when that part is randomly selected. This paper develops a theoretical explanation for this behavior through the Universal Winning Slice Hypothesis. It connects the usefulness of small subnetworks to properties already present in pretrained weights and representations.

The explanation has two components. Spectral balance means that different slices of weight matrices have remarkably similar eigenspectra. High task energy means that the pretrained backbone retains rich features relevant to downstream tasks. Together, these properties underpin the paper's framework for why a small selected slice can support effective adaptation.

The resulting method, SliceFine, updates selected portions of the original weights and adds no new parameters. Across the reported language and vision tasks, it matches state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning performance while improving training speed, memory efficiency, and model compactness. The work links an account of pretrained-model redundancy to a practical adaptation method that uses existing parameter capacity directly.
icml-2026-slicefine-the-universal-winnin.tldr: SliceFine adapts pretrained models by updating small slices of existing weights, supported by a theory of spectral balance and retained task information.

paragraphs: Many learning-theory bounds depend on the geometry of the data, including its intrinsic dimension, curvature, and reach. Testing those assumptions is difficult: simple analytic manifolds have known geometry but limited realism, while real datasets rarely permit precise geometric measurement. This paper builds a controlled benchmark between those extremes.

The authors extend dSprites and COIL-20 with additional transformation dimensions and dense sampling aligned with those dimensions. Finite-difference estimators then recover curvature, reach, and volume at near-ground-truth accuracy in the studied regime. That regime is one where general-purpose estimators can be unreliable or difficult to apply, making the controlled sampling a central part of the framework.

The benchmark serves as a calibration environment for geometric estimators and a testing ground for theoretical assumptions. Two application studies examine how existing bounds scale and how geometry changes across layers of a beta-VAE. These examples demonstrate how measurable data geometry can help assess current theory and guide future theoretical development with controlled evidence.
icml-2026-the-data-manifold-under-the-mi.tldr: A controlled image-data benchmark enables precise geometric measurements for calibrating estimators and examining assumptions behind learning theory.

paragraphs: Pruning weights and stopping a network early both save computation by using only part of a full calculation. This paper develops a shared theoretical view of those two strategies. It treats one-shot magnitude pruning as a fixed reduction in computation and early exit as a reduction that can adapt during evaluation.

In an asymptotic single-neuron model, the authors prove a concentration result for magnitude pruning with explicit rates. For early exit, they introduce a conditional perceptron and derive a power-law relationship between excess generalization error and the compute gap. The exponent increases without bound as partial and full computations become perfectly aligned.

The analysis then extends to deep networks, describing how distortions from pruning accumulate with depth. It also derives a compute–accuracy trade-off for early exit with a frozen backbone under a neural network Gaussian process model. Numerical simulations support the predicted scaling laws. These results make alignment between partial and full computation central to understanding when computation savings can preserve accuracy.
icml-2026-theoretical-guarantees-for-one.tldr: A unified theory relates pruning and early-exit accuracy to how closely partial computations match full computations.

paragraphs: A language model inside an image generator can encode words without reasoning about what those words imply visually. Think-Then-Generate makes reasoning and prompt rewriting part of image generation. The language encoder interprets the user's request, rewrites it, and supplies the rewritten prompt's internal states to condition the diffusion model.

Training begins with lightweight supervised fine-tuning to establish the reasoning-and-rewriting behavior. Dual-GRPO then jointly optimizes the language encoder and diffusion backbone. Image-grounded rewards encourage the encoder to use relevant world knowledge, while the diffusion component is trained toward semantic consistency and visually coherent rendering. This connects interpretation of the request with the image ultimately produced.

Across reasoning-oriented generation and editing benchmarks, the authors report substantial improvements in factual consistency, semantic alignment, and realism. The method reaches a WISE score of 0.79, described as nearly matching GPT-4. The results support explicit reasoning in the text-conditioning stage as a promising way to improve images whose correct depiction requires more than literal prompt encoding.
icml-2026-think-then-generate-reasoning-.tldr: Think-Then-Generate trains a language encoder to reason and rewrite prompts before diffusion, improving reasoning-dependent image generation and editing.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation reduces the cost of fine-tuning, but adapted models can still lose previously learned capabilities. This paper studies that forgetting through a simplified mean-field model of self-attention. In the model, tokens behave as interacting particles, and the LoRA update enters as a low-rank perturbation of their dynamics.

Using partial differential equations and dynamical-systems analysis, the authors identify regimes suggesting a transition between forgetting and non-forgetting behavior. One transition depends on the size of the perturbation, measured by its norm, and another depends on Transformer depth. The analysis therefore links forgetting to both the strength of adaptation and the extent of attention processing.

The authors also bound the time until the perturbed dynamics deviate, using perturbation size and spectral quantities. Experiments and exploratory analyses of real models under LoRA fine-tuning corroborate the predicted trends. The theoretical results concern a tractable toy model, while the real-model evidence connects its qualitative predictions to practical adaptation behavior.
icml-2026-understanding-catastrophic-for.tldr: A mean-field attention model links LoRA forgetting transitions to update magnitude and Transformer depth, with experiments supporting the predicted trends.

paragraphs: A Transformer may be able to represent a Boolean function yet struggle to learn it. The paper investigates this gap for sensitive functions, whose outputs frequently change when one input bit changes. Parity is a motivating example. The authors examine how much of parameter space corresponds to such functions.

Their analysis shows that sensitive functions can occupy vanishingly small regions of parameter space even when suitable parameter settings exist. Random initialization is therefore very likely to miss those regions. To explain this more precisely, the paper studies the full sensitivity profile: how sensitivity varies across individual inputs, rather than only its average across all inputs.

The authors prove that randomly initialized Transformers almost surely compute functions containing low-sensitivity input strings. Within the paper's theoretical account, functions lacking such strings are consequently unlearnable. The contribution is a geometric explanation for the representability–learnability gap: the existence of a correct parameter setting does not describe how much parameter-space volume supports the target behavior.
icml-2026-understanding-the-parameter-sp.tldr: The paper links Transformers' difficulty learning sensitive Boolean functions to the vanishing parameter-space volume occupied by those functions.

paragraphs: Many image-enhancement methods use stochastic processes to transform degraded inputs, but their relationship to standard diffusion models can be unclear. This paper organizes these approaches into three families: unconditional diffusion models, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, and diffusion bridges. It shows that all three fit a common stochastic differential equation formulation.

The framework identifies the mathematical choices separating the methods: drift and diffusion terms, terminal distributions, and boundary conditions. It also separates those choices from schedulers and samplers, which can be varied independently. This organization makes it easier to identify what a proposed method actually changes and to compare alternatives on shared terms.

The authors conduct controlled experiments across multiple enhancement tasks using identical architectures and training protocols. No method consistently dominates; the study instead disentangles design choices that strongly affect performance. They also release ItoVision, a modular PyTorch implementation of the framework. Together, the theory, controlled comparisons, and library support fairer evaluation and more systematic experimentation with stochastic image enhancement.
icml-2026-unifying-deep-stochastic-proce.tldr: A common stochastic-equation framework unifies image-enhancement methods and enables controlled comparisons that find no consistently dominant approach.

paragraphs: Saliency maps highlight image regions associated with a model's prediction, but similar maps can sometimes come from trained and randomized networks. This paper identifies an architectural explanation for part of that resemblance. Common convolutional design choices create a tendency to emphasize the image center, even before meaningful learning occurs.

Controlled ablations connect this bias to zero padding and receptive-field growth. The center emphasis appears in randomly initialized convolutional networks and with randomized inputs. It is largely absent in the studied non-convolutional architectures, including Vision Transformers and multilayer perceptrons. These observations show that a visually structured saliency map can partly reflect network design.

The authors introduce a corner-shift benchmark and a Center-Shift Index to measure how saliency changes when objects move. Training can partially redirect saliency toward object regions, while randomized models remain dominated by the center bias. This provides one mechanism that inflates trained–random similarity and shows why saliency evaluations need to distinguish learned responses from architectural spatial preferences.
icml-2026-when-random-saliency-looks-tra.tldr: Convolutional design choices can create center-focused saliency before training, confounding comparisons between trained and randomized networks.
